questions.q: What is the literal meaning of the child's opening line "डकस डकस वपन्ज उघा फुघरह" (Dark dark letters don't catch/hold)?
questions.a: The child expresses that the written letters appear dark, indistinct, and impossible to grasp or retain—he cannot "catch" their meaning. A wrong answer (e.g., "The child hates books") reveals the student is imposing an emotional judgment instead of staying with the sensory, tactile metaphor the child uses; it shows confusion between literal imagery and thematic interpretation.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the child says "मैं तो नहीं पढ़ूँगा" (I will not read) even after the poet explains the benefits of literacy.
questions.a: The child rejects literacy because it belongs to a world (the city, the "dydÙkk") that demands he leave his mother, his village, and his identity; he sees no value in a skill that uproots him. A wrong answer (e.g., "He is lazy/stubborn") reveals the student views the child through a deficit lens, missing the poem's critique of education as cultural displacement and the child's agency in protecting his belonging.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "speaker vs. poet" to this poem: Identify two stanzas where the *speaker* is the child and two where the *speaker* is the poet. How does this shift in voice structure the theme?
questions.a: Child speaks in stanzas 1, 3, 5 (e.g., "डकस डकस...", "पैक कहती है...", "पैक बोली..."); poet speaks in stanzas 2, 4, 6 (e.g., "मैंने कहा...", "पैक ने कहा...", "पैक पढ़ी..."). The alternating voices create a dialogue that structures the theme as a *conflict* rather than a monologue, forcing the reader to weigh both worldviews. A wrong answer that attributes all lines to the poet shows inability to distinguish dramatic voices, leading to a flattened reading where the child's resistance disappears.

questions.q: Analyze the significance of the child's final statement: "द्यदूक्क इक त्ज फ्जस" (On the city's forehead I will spit / throw a challenge). How does this image transform the poem's primary theme from "resistance" to "assertion"?
questions.a: The verb "ctj fxjs" (spitting/challenging) turns passive refusal into active defiance; the city becomes a tangible opponent, and the child claims power over his destiny. The theme shifts from *being excluded by literacy* to *rejecting the city's terms*. A wrong answer that reads it as mere anger misses the symbolic reclamation of agency—the child defines his own "signature" (ctj) instead of accepting the city's script.

questions.q: Evaluate the poet's stance: Does Fakyakspu ultimately side with the child's refusal or with the necessity of literacy? Defend your judgment using the poet's own words in the penultimate stanza ("पैक पढ़ लेना अच्छा है...").
questions.a: The poet *empathizes* with the child (he records the child's logic without mockery) but *does not endorse* the refusal; he gently insists "पैक पढ़ लेना अच्छा है" (it is good to read) because he knows the city's power is inescapable. The message is tragic empathy: the poet sees the child's world as valid but doomed. A wrong answer claiming the poet "supports illiteracy" ignores the poet's persistent coaxing; one claiming he "fully supports modernity" ignores the tender preservation of the child's voice.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza in Hindi (or English) that could serve as an alternate ending to the poem, where the child *chooses* to learn—but on his own terms. Your stanza must use one metaphor from the original poem (e.g., "dark letters," "city's forehead," "mother's lap").
questions.a: Example: "अब मैं पकडूँगा डकस डकस अकसर / माँ की गोद में बैठकर सीखूँगा घर / शहर के माथे पर नहीं, अपनी माटी पर / लिखूँगा अपना नाम, नई सुबह बनाकर।" A good answer retains the child's agency and recontextualizes the metaphor. A poor answer simply has the child obey ("मैं पढूँगा") without transforming the power dynamic, showing the student hasn't internalized the theme of *self-determination*.
